Revolution in Spain, and Fai.t. or Espartero. þÿ One of the most important revolutions since that of France in 1830. and that of Belgium, which placed Leopold upon the throne, has occurred during the course of the past week in the fall of the Regent Espartero, and the triumph of the parties united against hint ; an event, important not only as regards Spain itself, but as affecting, as it most likely will do, the general peace ol Europe. The most extraordinary, and indeed the most frightful feature in this revolution is, the manner and instrument by which 't has been effected ; comprehending, as it does, the two characteristic features of the awful precedent of the French Revolution ; the total revolt of the army, and the fraternisation of the army of the state with the army of the rebels against which it was led. In all the nations of Europe, the public peace and the authority ol the law, and particularly in times of general discontent, must ultimately rest ori, and can only be maintained by, the public force or army of the state, and therefore the discipline, and above all, the loyalty and obedience of the army, are of the first moment to the very safety of a government, and form the sole and paramount security for the existence of all civil institutions. The dissolution of military discipline and military obedience is therefore one of the most awful circumstances in the present case of the Spanish monarchy ; and w hen we consider that the like spirit of popular discontent þÿ like in i' s nature, though

happily not in its degree þÿ pervades other countries besides Spain, we cannot look without the most serious apprehension to the perilous nature of the example of this military revolt, this sudden defection of the whole army from its proper commander and the government, and this fraternisation, to adopt the French term, ot the army of the state with the rebels against whom it was led. The circumstances of this revolt lie, unhappily, in a very small compass The two opponent armies meet in front of the capital ; but instead of lighting, they immediately open their ranks and fraternise with each other. Tne gates of the capital are thrown open, and the contest is over. E-partero is deserted and left to his fate, and the mutinous army tuid their leaders become masters of the kingdom. No blood is shed, because the revolt is general ; not a single regiment remains faithful to 'he government and the Regent : all become traitors and mutineers to a man. The latest accounts from Madrid state that the Lopez ministry has been re constituted, and that the national guards have been disarmed. M. Arguelles the guardian of the Queen, has resigned his office. The course which the revolutionary government will take is at present a matter of uncertainty, hat it is supposed that it will immediately recall the Cortes Intel v dissolved by Bspartero: 'I he Queen will then be declared of an age to contract a marriage, and u husband, in the usual

MST&MSTDS AT13 manner of a royal alliance, will tie proposed for her upon the meeting of the Cortes. '1 he first prince on the list, it is said, will he the I'rutee of Astoria, ihe eldest son of I >nn Carlos He will be rejected, it is said, as a matter of course. The son of Don I' tan ei<co lie Paulo (who has rnanv friends) will be then brought forward and put aside by the Cortes. " Another and another slill the princes of Lucca aod of Naples will meet the same fate, and ilien will come an appeal to all good Spaniaids to terminate all the evils of Spain - and to secure her future peace þÿ by assenting to the bestowal of the hand of their Queen upon the Due d'Autnale, þÿ and this will be done, it remains to he seen whether Louts Philippe will he enabled to withstand this snlendid temptation for the aggrandisement of In nisei f and familv. if the Cortes and Spanish nation should thus solicit ttie alliance, an i should represent it as the onlv means of restoring tranquility to the kingdom. We must leave this matter where it is; all that is known for certain is. that t lie kingdom is in the possession of a revolted army, and that Espartero is a fugitive.

ALARMING STATE OF SOUTH WALES. We regret to state that this portion of the Principality still continues in vety lit. settled a condition. The government have, we under stand, sent down Mr. liall the magistrate, to institute an inquiry into the cause of the (lis turbances. A portion of the A division of police have also been dispatched lo eo operate with the local authorities and the military. þÿ There appears to have been a desperate affray, in an attempt made by Ca-ptain Napier, the chief constable ol Carmarthenshire, assisted bv Inspector Rees, of the Swansea police, and two men, to capture some parties who had been concerned in the destination of a gate. At a meeting of the mngistrafes on Tuesday, it was agreed that a regular country police force should he organised, as one of the most effectual means of putting an end to the present outrages. It seemed to be generally admitted that the farmers were labouring tinder severe grievances, and that, in some instances, gates had been erected where they had no right to he, and a desire was expressed that these wrongs should be redressed ; hut that it would not do to allow the parlies to take the law into their own hands, and indulge in a blind and sweeping system of revenge.

WRECK OF THE PEGASUS STEAMþÿES UPWARDS OF FIFTY LlVES LOST. We deeply regret to have to record the loss of the Pegasus steamer, plying between Le 1 1 h and Hull The disastrous occurrence took place at one o'clock on Thursday morning, in the i eighbourhood of the spot where the Forfarshire steamer was wrecked five years ago, and where the late Grace Darling immortalised herself by the heroic devotion with which she perilled her own life in the successful attempt to save the lives of five of the passengers who were clinging to the rocks. The number of lives lost by the wreck of the Pegasus has not yet been ascertained, as no list was kept of the steerage passengers, but there can be no doubt that the number exceeds 50. All on board, both passengers and crew, with the exception of six individuals, have unhappily perished. The vessel, which was built iu the Clyde, in 1835> and was of 130 horse power, had only left Letth about eight hours before the fearful catastrophe happened.

THE FATE OF THE COLUMBIA. We have learned the following additional particulars respect ini this vessel, from which it appears that it has become a total wreck. This disaster is the third which the vessels composing the line have sustained since its establishment, three years ago, and we are glad to tind, from the unanimous testimony of all on board, that not the slightest bltm-e is attributable to Captain Shannon, the commander. The Columbia went on shore about one þÿo clock on the afternoon of Sunday, the 2nd instant, on the þÿDevil L s imb (a solid rock), a mile and a quarter from land, and one and a half from the lighthouse on Seal Island, which lies a few miles west of Cape Sable, and is about 130 miles from Halifax. The unfortunate occurrence is attributed to the unusually strong current setting into the Bay of Dundy, with the dense fog that prevailed. The inset is described as having been stronger than was ever before remembered. A brig went on shore on the following dav, near the same spot, and some other disasters have occurted From the thickness of the fog, nothing at a distance was discernible, and, consequently, ft was impossible to form any accurate judgment as to their particular situation. For three hours the fate o! those on hoard was a matter of considerable anxiety, and tlte impending danger continued to assume a more fearful aspect. During this time every exertion was making to lighten the vessel by throwing the coal, fr.c.., into the sea ; ami with her engines and every available means

a continued perseverance was made to get her off, but without success. Alarm guns were constantly fired, hut, unfortunately, from ignorance of their position, at the side of the ship from the shore. About four þÿo clock a boat from the island made its appearance, ami very quickly explained to them their þÿ whereabouts." The ladies were all immediately sent on shore ; most of the other passengers remained until the next morning, for the purpose of rendering whatever assistance they could towards saving the ship. At every flood tide the engine was put in operation, with a view of backing her, but the impracticability of moving her may be conceived from the fact, that she was so far upon tfie rock as to draw at her bows five feet of water less than usual. All the passengers 80 in number, and the crew, except one man missing, were safely landed on Beal Island. The þÿpassengers luggage, and. indeed, all tho moveables, were also got safely to land, and part of the coals Messrs. Cunard, on learntrig this unpleasant news, at once set to work to equip the steam ship Margaiet, kept at Halifax as a reserve ship, and she soon set out for Seal Island, and on her arrival found the Columbia in such a position as showed that there was very little chance of saving alight but the machinery. The timbers were fast giving wav, and every moment increased the water i.'i her hold. On Wednesday she broke her bank, and, when the Margaret left, was swinging by the bows, and certain, from the least violent commotion of the wind and

waves, to become utterly destroyed A meeting of the passengers was held at Seal Island, and a resolution was passed, appointing a commit teemf five to draw up a letter to Captain Shannon, expressing then high opinion of ins conduct. The letter was subsc-

His Excellency the Governor General arrived here on the 2d inst , and yesterday reviewed the Military and the Militia þÿ we were happy to observe that His Excellency appeared high in health and spirits, and to be well pleased with the appearance, bearing and conduct of the Military and Militia corps. The enthusiastic cheers to the men when His Excellency retired, which startled almost our little town from its propriety, must have been gratifying as an index that his mild and lenient rule is appreciated as it ought to be. His Excellency the Governor General left this morning for the Island of St. John. þÿ »coo» þÿ (Prom our Correspondent at St. Thomas.) JAMAICA. DREADFUL CONFLAGRATION AND DESTRUCTION OF PROF DUTY. At about noon on Saturday 2Gth Aug a fire broke outat Sanies' Foundry, situate at the South East part of Kingston, Jamaica. The sea breeze was then blowing very strong, which caused the flames to spread northward with almost incredible rapidity, and speedily reduced to ashes a vast amount of property. The fire continued its course in this direction until towards night, when the wind changed, and with it the course of the (ire, which now took the direction from whence it first originated, and ere the hour of midnight, hundreds of houses which a few short hours before afforded shelter to their occupants, were reduced to ashes. The loss of property is estimated at £400,000, and which has fallen heavily on the owners of property in the eastern part of the city, extending in a

northerly direction, to the extent of a quarter of a mile The feelings of sympathy for those who have suffered and the distress which prevails among the sufferers have spread a gloom, and caused business of every description to be almost entirely neglected. The fire had very nearly destroyed the whole town þÿ the destitution of the poor people who are burnt out is exceedingly great and there will be great suffering in Kingston þÿ the business part of the city has providentially been saved, as there would have been great famine.

Spain. þÿ It is reported that Espartero is on his wav to the English coast in search of refuge, and possibly i.i the expectation of some mediation or interference on his behalf. Most heartily do we wisn that it could he afforded without involving the country in the peril of war ; but humanity and generosity themselves must be corrected and controlled by sound discretion, and we must not incur the peril of a war to reinstate an exiled Regent, however oppressodlv arid dishonourably treated. Ekpnrtero has always been the friend of England, and has been assisted by such friendly offices of our government as Could be afforded without any unauthorised Intervention tn the internal affairs of a friendly foreign power. Some of otlr journals have assailed him, and we think rather harshly, for his bombardment of Seville. Rut what choice had he 7 þÿ

a>A»3« Tsstmaasat assMarnsrea ma. He was placed in this dilemma, either of do ing nothing, and passively filing before his enemies, or of attempting to do whatever appeared to be in hiS power. He and fits army were in front of Seville before General Narvaez had succeeded in getting possession of Madrid The city of Seville shut its gates against him, though the officers and a greater portion of the garrison had declared in fiis favour. Accordingly, he ordered an immediate attack, and it is obvious that he would have taken the city if he had not raised the siege upon receiving the intelligence of the loss of Madrid. He then retreated upon Cadiz and being pursued by a superior force, and not admitted into the garrison, as lie expected, he sought refuge ou board a British ship of war. The latest news from Madrid does not furnish us w ith any iutefligence of importance. A good deal of dissension exists amongst the leaders of the successful party respecting the course which they shall now pursue ; and some of the provincial juntas seem determined not to submit to the orders ol the new Cabinet.
LOSS OF HER MAJESTY'S WAR - STEAMER LIZARD. Letters have heeti received conveying t he

War steamer Lizard, which occurred lue on the night of the 24ih or eaily on i.ie morning of the 25Ui uit., by her having tieen i unclean by the French war steamer Verne e, about 25 nnles to the eastward of onualiar, while on her passage thence to Udiceluna fi appta.s that the Lizard left Gibraltar on the evening of Monday, the 24th. with the w ind blowing moderately from the southward, which freshened towards midnight, and the atmosphere became dark and clouded. VVitnin a few minutes of the collision, the look out men on board the Lizard descried a steamer beanug down upon them, and they immediately made signals to and flailed the approaching vessel. The crew oh board the French steamer evidently could not have seen the signals, or fieard the hailing, as she kept on her course, and run right into the Lizard, striking her with tremendous force nearly amidships, and close to her engine-room. The concussion was so great that many of the þÿLizard crew s were thrown down by its violence. It was immediately discovered that the vessel had sustained some very serious damage, as the water was pouring rapidly into her, and upon further examination it was found that any exertions on the part of her crcw> to keep her afloat would be utterly useless, as she was then in a sinking state. Nevertheless, every possible means were resorted to by the olficers and men to Save the ship until the water gained upon her so much that it extinguished her fires, and her machinery consequently became powerless The French steamer did

not sustain any serious damage, and Seeing the condition of the Lizard, remained by her. in order to render any assistance in her power. When all hope Of saving the Lizard was abandoned, the attention of her officers was directed to the preservation of the ship's company, which was happily accomplished without the loss of a single life, by the boa's conveying all hands in safety on board the Veloee. Scarcely had the last of the crew reached the French Steamer, and within two hours of the collision, when the Lizatd sunk. The Veloee proceeded to Gibraltar with the crew of the Lizard, where they were received on board her Majesty's ship Indus, 72.

Though the lives of the officers and þÿship s company of the Lizard were fortunately preserved, yet everything they possessed on board was lost, as was also the þÿship s tores, furniture, &c. The Lizard has been a considerable time in the Mediterranean, and was the sister ship to the Locust, both of which were employed as tenders, between Gibraltar and Malta, and were considered two of the best and fastest vessels of their class in the service.

We have to record another fatal steam boat accident, which occurred about a quarter to one o'clock on Monday morning ofT Dungeness, The Fluton, a first rate war steamer belonging to the French government, when off Hurigeness, while going at full speed, ran into the starboard quarter of the Jane, of Sunderland, from Newcastle, bound to Rouen, with coals. Such was the force of the collision that the steamer tore away the chains, rigging, and everything within »each of her bows. One poor fellow named G. Lawrenson, the mate of the schooner, was crushed to death between the main chains and the þÿSteamer b s ows, and his body carried overboard. The master, J. intelligence ol the total loss of her May þÿsty s Carder, and the rest of the crew, jumped intd the boat that was being towed at the schooner's Stern, which went down by the head almost at the moment that the painter was cut. After rowing for some time they came up with the Fluton, and were taken on board, and on being landed on Wednesday morning at Woolwich received 3s. to pay their passage to London. Foundering of a Vessel With all Hands. þÿ The melancholy intelligence of the total shipwreck of the brig Falcon of London, with the loss of all her crew, excepting one seaman, has been received. She is stated to have been a line vessel of about 150 tons burden,

and the number who have so unfortunately perished amount to 13, including the master, Captain Cairns. The information was received by a letter written by Captain Burgess, of the brig Athelstan, dated Archangel, June 27. The subjoined is an extract : þÿ þÿ Before we find scarcely made Norrh Cape, we saw a brig apparently saiiing towards us with signal colours of distress; vve immediately hauled towards her in the hope of rendering her assistance. We ascertained her to be the Falcon, Captain Cairns, of London, ana the ciew informed us that she had struck on on a sunken rock Feeling alarmed for their safety, I instantly begged of the master to inform me what he intended to do, but whether from flight or otherwise, he gave me no answer The next moment our sails were filled and went a bend of him, and had down both topsails to reef. Having the navigation of my own vessel to mind, and giving directions to my crew respecting the sails, my attention for a short period was withdrawn from the brig In the mean time she had run close under our lee, hove her maintopsail aback, and put her helm down. In consequence of her so doing in the short space of time of two minutes we were alongside of each other, a very heavy sea running at the time. All in a moment we heard exclamations from the Crow that the Falcon was going down, and pieicing cries wore made lor ropes and such assistance ns we could possibly aflbrd them Ropes were instantly thrown to them, hut she was too far gone, ns in the
next moment she went down with the whole of the crew, With the exception of one man, who had n miraculous escape in getting tn board our vessel.- Ibid.

O Thou great and gracious Being! To all Creatures ever kind ! Source of vision to the Seeing, Friend and Father of the Blind.
Joys of Sight ! they are denied us ; Let Thy holy will be done! In our blindness Thou wilt guide us, Thou, O God, our Light, our Sun.
Thro' the sounds that fall and linger On the eager, þÿlist ning ear, þÿThro the quick discerning finger, Bidding darkness disappear.
þÿTf.ro the friends whom Thou hast given, And whose hearts Thy love controls, Thou art pouring down from Heaven, þÿLearning light s upon our souls.
Now, no ills our hearts shall sadden, They shall know no painful fears ; Though our eyes no sun beams gladden, They shall stream no more with tears.

The followers of the Regent, ; least the few who proved faithful in the ours of adversitv, were almost entirely destroyed by the volleys ot the enemy at the moment of embarkation. The Regent embarked in a common launch and succeeded in reaching the English fine of Battle Ship Malabar, at the time laying in the Cadiz road; it appears that the commander Captain Sartorius was undecided of the mode of reception, which would be given to the exile, but on the receipt of a cornrnu nication from the British Consul at Cadiz, the yards of the Malabar were manned and a salute of 14 guns was fired in honor of the Regent. The escort of the Regent had 8 killed and 50 wounded, and the Regent nar rowiy escaped þÿcapture -his brother was made a prisoner þÿ the Malabar immediately sailed for Lisbon. A Correspondent states that means for terminating the differences respecting the marriage ol the Queen have been discussed, and approved of by both the British and French Governments, who are now in perfec t accord on the subject. Her Majesty is neither to wed a prince of the House of Coburg, nor a prince of the House of Orleans, but the son of her uncle Don

INDIA AND CHINA. EXTRAORDINARY EXPStF,1;?, The Bombay Mail of the of June has arrived. Tire intelligence which it brings is of interest, and in particular relative to the state ol the newly acquired pro-

vince of Scir.de. That most fertile district which under a good government and properly cultivated will become a garden, i now nearly pacified by the measures adopt, ed by Sir Charles Napier, its present gov. erwrr. He has made terms with most cC the Chiefs, and even Meer Shere Mahomed is stated to have offered to make his submission provided he could have his private property secuted to him. There is no doubt that within a short time the complete pacification of the country will be effected. Sickness prevailed very much in the camp at Hyderabad. Several Ofliceis died. Sir Charles Napier had an attack ef fever but had recovered. The communications by sea with Scinde had been closed by the monsoon, but the route via Omercote to BliOoj and Balrneer would, it was expected be speedily' opened. The navigation of the Indus from Lukkur to Hyderabad was uninterrupted, and the camp .at Hyderabad was abundantly supplied with food and ammunition, and every other necessary. The provinces of Scinde, which very much resembles Egypt, are usually flooded by the rivers and canals during the monsoon ; they wui require little more than common care to produce an extraordinary revenue. The amount once tar exceeded 1,000,00015 sterling, and it is to be expected that it will soon again reach that sum. The subsiding of the waters will, it is feared, unless proper precautions arc taken, increase he sickness of the troops, but, the Genoa! is experienced, there is a well founded expectation that

the due precaution will be adopted. There was an absurd rumour got up about a confederacy having been firmed among the northern and Jbikh chiefs at Subathoo against the British, but its extravagance wa3 speedily discovered. One of the most remarkable events of the month is the solemn protest of the officers of the army at Hyderabad against the calumnies of the Bombay Times, winch paper accused them of having dishonoured the Zenana of the ex Ameers. They presented an address to Sir Charles Napier praying for protection against those calumnies, and they received a decided reply from their General. The address, and reply have been published in the journals of Bombay, and were to be also circulated throughout India. The ex Ameers had been removed from Bombay to Sassour, n< ar Poonah The most dangerous of them was a prisoner in the Castle of Surat, where he was well guarded.

INSURRECTION IN SPAIN. We regret to repot t that the insurrection has become general in the provinces of Valencia and Catalonia. The accounts fiorn the other provinces are favourable to the government It is suflioient to sav of the character and grounds of tiiis insurrection, that it is a mere republican and anaichical movement ; another effort at revolution amongst a people, whom long habits of insurrection have rendered impatient of all control, and restless under anything like peace, security, and establishment Esparteio. however, has met his difficulties with correspondent firmness and resolution, and has issued a manifesto, in which he declares Ins purpose to defend the institutions of the kingdom, and in obe.t Mice to Ins oath, as Regent, to die in the field, if necessary, in defence of the Queen and the constitutional government. It remains to he scon whether lhe army will remain faithful to their general, of which great doubts are entertained, but none whatever of ;|ie vigour and spirit of the Regent himself, and, to do him justice, of Ins moderation and fidelity. Tiie next accounts will, perhaps, determine the issue of the matter; the success ot Espartero, or a new, and we fear a sanguinary revolution, in this unhappy monarchy, 'lhe latest accounts which we have received state that the Regent had left .Madrid for Valencia, accompanied by Generals Linage and Feunz, and the war minister, 'l he troops of the garrison have also left Madrid, the pence of which is confided to the National Guard

On Tuesday morning as the locker of a warehouse, situated itt Dundee stieel, Liverpool, was proceeding, according to his usual custom, to open the concern, he discovered inside the front or main entrance a piece of of cotton with some luciter matches in the centre. The cotton bore evident marks of having been ignited, for it was partially burnt round the edges t and as it was placed about the length of a þÿman s arm inside the hole in the doorway, which is called the cat-hole, and which has been made lor the pui pose of affording ingress and egress lor cats and also for rats, there cannot exist any dount but that it was so placed by some wickedly disposed villain or villains, for the purpose of setting fire to the premises. The anempt was, however, most providentially defeated, owing to the cotton not having continued to burn after it had become ignited, 't he ware house which has thus been preserved fiorn destruction is one of a pile ol several magnificent structures of the same description recently erected, at very considerable cost, in Dundee street At present they contain some thousands of bales ot cotton, and a large quantity ol palm oil þÿ materials ol such a combustible nature, that had the diabolical attempt been successful, the probability is that the whole pile would have been in ruins before many hours were at an end Shortly after tire discovery the magistrates ol the borough were summoned to attend a meeting

at the Sessions house, to institute an investigation, and adopt such measures as might be considered advisable under the circumstances. As the proceedings were conducted with strict secrecy, we are not in a position to enter into any detailed particulars ; but the new discovery seemed more confidently than ever before to impress all of them wnfi the belief that many of tiie late fires have been the work of a gang ol incendiaries, and that precautionary measures will be rendered comparatively valueless untill the gang in question shall have been discovered and visited witli die condign punishment which the extent and atrocity of their crimes so justly deserve. It is gratifying to know that all parties are fully alive to the exigencies of the case. The auiboriiies, the commercial associations, fire insurance companies, and, indeed, the inhabitants generally, are meeting, and evincing the most anxious desire to co operate one with the oilier m checking an evil ol the portentous magnitude which this has become, every man feeling that Ins own interests and the interests of those around him must lie materially injured unless safety for propei ty can be secured. The slate, however, ot apprehension and uncertainty which overspread the town is truly deplorable. Every night fresh intelligence of the breaking out ol a lire in one quarter or another is expected, and of such frequent occurrence have those con flagraiions become, that when the intelligence respecting them arrives it creates little or no

surprise. Tremendous Flood þÿ Tiirf.b Bridges The lute heavy rains have caused the swelling of the rivers to such un extent that last Friday a torrent of water from the mountains swept down the vale of Gwiiiy, with irresistible force, and completely filled

the vale of Towy for miles with one vast sheet of water. It destroyed entirely die Troedyrhiw, Cwmgwilly, and Glangwilly bridges, the fiisi and last being very slumgly built with stone, while that at Cwmgwdly is a wooden one. Tire Glangwilly budge is so completely destroyed, that scarcely a ve«tigc of it is left. Tan of the culvert of Abergvnlly budge is also gone, and on Saturday the Gloucester mail passed over it on planks laid there during the night. Some idea of the impetuosity of the torrent may be formed Irom the fact that the rivers were seen advancing bodily, like a wall, about six yards in height and coni inning in that ioim for some time. The inhabitants of the lower fields near Carmarthen had scarcely time to drive their cattie to a place of shelter, when the whole vale was filled. Air. T. The Sufferers nt Fall Hirer. þÿ A committee of tfie citizens of Fall River have published a circular asking for assistance to the sullerers by the late destructive fire at that place, as follows : þÿ CIRCULAR. To their feiiow citizens, near and remote, boih in town and country, the undersigned, a committee in behalf of the people of Fall River, Mass., make this their brie! appeal for help, and the appalling calamity, which, under the wise and righteous Providence of God, has overtaken us. (Jur population, from 8000 to 9000 souls, and chiefly devoted to manufacturing and mechanic pursuits, is in deep þÿdistress a portion of it in pressing want. At 4 þÿo clock, P. M. last Sabbath, the 2d mst., a fire broke out in a central pail of tliis village, (the wind was blowing a guie.) winch, in its ravages, was of the must dt-so laiing character. The burnt district comprises some fifteen or twenty acres of the centre ol business operations. Nearly 200 buildings (not including many small ones) are consumed ; among which are thiee newly built houses ot public worship, and all our public offices Uur post office and custom house are gone, and wo have not a printing office, nor hotel, nor bank building, nor book stoie, nor market, nor bakeiv lelt. Neatly ail our grocery and provisions stores, including one wholesale establishment, with most of their contents; and all our drygoods, druggist, tailor, milliner, tin ware, and paint shops, with one cotton factory, running 3000 spindles, are gone.

Nearly two hundred families are turned houseless, and many of them penny less, into the streets. Besides, tins appalling lire raged with sucli fury, and spread with such velocity, that many of the sufferers gladly escaped with their lives, without a pillow for their heads, or a change of raiment for their backs. The amount of property consumed it is impossible to estimate, even by anything like a probable approximation. The assessors of the town, in the discharge of their official duties, within the last two months, have rated the property of the place at three and a half millions of þÿdollars and the heart of the village is in ashes. We cannot, we need not enlarge. We tell you, in lew words, the simple, sad story of our calamity ; and with the scene of desolation before us> and the cries of distress around us, we ask your aid. In behalf of our suffering neighbors, and in the name of humanity and o! our Heavenly Father, we appeal to your kindness and your love, and solicit your assistance : not to repair our losses and rebuild our village, but to relieve our present distress, and enable us to give bread to the hungry, clothing to the naked, and shelter to the houseless ; until, w ith due eflnrt on the part of all among us, a merciful and righieous God, who lias justly allliclerl us, shall command the bum of business, the smile of contentment, and the song of joy to return to our now desolate bottlers. (Send us what you can þÿsend food,

clothing, money þÿ send it addressed to either of os, and it shall be carefully distributed to tfie needy. N. A MISER. The following account of Michael Biard or Baer) who lately lived near Little York, Penn., is extracted from the Belmont Penn.) Repository. Mr. B. was of German extraction . His father left him a valuable farm of five hundred acres, in the vicinity of York, with some farming and household articles. He kept a tavern for a number of years þÿ married a wife and raised four children He accumulated an immense estate, which he preserved so tenaciously that he never offered a dollar for the, education of his family. He was never known to lay out one dollar in cash far any article he might be in want of ; he would either do without it, or find some person who would barter with him for something he could not conveniently sell for money. He farmed largely, and kept a large distillery, which he supplied entirely with his own grain. He kept a team for the conveyance of his whiskey and flour to Baltimore, which, when he could not sell for money at a price to suit him, he bartered for necessaries fur his family and. tavei n. In this way he amassed an estate wot th four hundred thousand dollars. Such was ins attachment to money that he never was known to lend or credit a dollar to any man. Upon the best mortgage or other secut ity that could be given, he would not lend a cent. He never vested one dollar in any of the public funds. Neither would he keep the notes of any bank longer than till he, could get them changed. He. deposited his specie in a large iron chest, until it would hold no more.

He, then provided a strong iron hooped barrel, which he also filled. After his death, his strong boxes, from whose, bourn no traveller had ever returned, yielded two hundred and thirty thousand dollars in gold and silver. The cause of hts death was as remarkable as the course of his life,. A gentleman from Virginia offered him twelve dollars per bushel for 110 bushels of clover seed; but he won l not sell it for less than thirteen dollars, and they did not agree. The seed was after Ward sent to Philadelphia, where it sold for seven dollars per bushel, and five hundred and fifty dollars less than the Virginian had offered for it On receiving an account of this sole, he walked through his farm, went to his distillery, and gave various directions to his people. He then went to his wagon house and hanged himself.

Type Setting þÿMachine. At a recent meet ing of the London Society Arts, Mr. Young of one of the inventors of the type setting machine, explained the construction and uses of the several parts of this contrivance. One of the machines being in the room, the inventor was enabled to show it in full work. The upper part consists of the type reservoirs, which are long rectangular channels, fixed in an inclined position to prevent the letters falling out, and of a size corresponding with that of the type to be used. Immediately below these reservoirs, are as many knives or cullers, the use of which is to cut off or displace the bottom letter of each column of type. The motion is given to these cutters, by the manipulation of the performer sitting in front of the. instrument, who in playing on the keys (altogether 96 in number) draws down the vertical rods, connecting the keys and the cutters, and thus displaces the cutters, which, pressing against the lowest letter of each column of type, causes it to pass through an opening in the bed plate of the cutters, and thus enter on to the top oi an inclined plane at the back of the machine. The inclined plane is constructed of brass, and contains several curlvilincal channels, down which the

At the bottom of the inclined plane is an eccentric movement (worked by a treadle) to regulate the admission of the stream of type into a long open trough or channel leading to the composing case, where tiie type is adjusted ready to form into pages lor the press. VV hen in full w ork, as many as 8000 letters, &c., may be set up by this machine worked by two young women, in one hour þÿ whereas, by tfte ordinary mode, a good compositor cannot set up more, on an average, than 1700 letters.

Christian Ike Eighth, 1 by the Grace of God, King of Denmark, of the Vandals and Goths, Duke of Sleswick, Holstein, Slormarn , Ditmarsken, Latienhurg and Oldenburg. OU!i SPECIAL FAVOR ! From your report, of the result of the transactions carried on by you, in obedience to Our Rescript of the 1st of May 1840, with the Planters of Our West India Islands, We have learned to Our Royal satisfaction, how the greatest pait of the Planters have more or less met Our paternal purpose of ameliorating the condition of the unfree Labourers. Whilst We perfectly agree in the acknowledgment, expressed bv so many, that it is both suitable and ad vantageous to the well understood interest of the Proprietors themselves, that also the spiritual welfare of tire unfree population is taken care of, by the application of Sundays and Holy-days, according to their Chi istian destination, as days of devotion and rest, it is, for the attainment of tins object. Our most gracious will and command : a, that the markets, which, notwithstanding the tenor of the 4th of the Edict of February 3rd 1755, issued immediately after the acquisition of the Islands by the State, have been tolerated on Sundays, shall henceforward be transferred to Saturday ; b, that the Kumshops on Sundays and Holydays shall be closed until 2 o'clock p. m. c, that the unfree Labourers shall not work for hire on Sundays and Hclv days, unless the competent Authorities, in indispensably necessary cases, which do not admit of delay, give their special permission to this

effect, and shall in such case the master have preference with regard to his own negroes and d, that they likewise, on such days, shall not work on or cultivate the pieces of ground allotted to them, during divine service, from 9 þÿo clock a. m. to 2 þÿo clock p in. In conjunction with the above, it is Our most gracious will and command to you, that you cause it to be taken into consideration, if any other measures might be adopted, for the purpose of the application of Sundays and Holy-days by the Unfree to religious reading and such instruction, as would tend to foster their Christian faith and to impart useful knowledge lo them. Whereas it is quite necessary, that the unfree Labourers receive compensation for the loss, they will suffer, in consequence of the above, with respect to their means of earning for themselves, it is, moreover, whilst We appreciate the readiness with which a great part of the Planters have declared themselves willing to make the sacrifices, requisite to the attainment of this object, Our most gracious will and command, that every Saturday shall be given to the mentioned Unfree as a free day, hut under the following restrictions: a, that every Unfrce, who in the course of the week, has been lying in the Sickhouse, if there he, according to the Physician's declaration, well-founded supposition of his not really having been sick, shall on the free day of the same week and the following Sunday remain as convalescent in the Sickhouse ; b, that the free-day may he withheld from
such Unfice, as in ihe course of the week,

If the Pioprietor or Administrator be of opinion, that a negro, who already has been punished three times in the same quarter u ilh the forfeiture of the free-day, has anew deserv ed this punishment, or d the same, on any Estate, have been applied so often, in the course of the quarter, that the punishments, taken together, in amount would exceed the number of the gang, the decision of the matter is to be releried to a Commissi m, to be appointed by the Governor General, and shall this Commission consist of ihe Poiicemuster ami two respectable Piauteis ot the Jurisdiction, but here must be ousel ved, that no Planter paiticipatcs in the judgment ol matters, that relate to Ins own Estate, and shall the Commission enter their decision into a Protocol, to be kept lor this purpose. .Should any negro consider himself wronged by the punishment inflicted on him, shall the right

to complain in this as well as in other cases be reserved to turn, it being the duty of Our Governor General also m this respect to prevent abuse and to take the necessary' steps lor the protection ol the Unfree; c, that the throwing of Grass on Saturday morning and evening, and Sunday evening shall he continued, as tiitherio has been the custom ; that also such other labours, as are indispensably necessary, are likewise to be executed as hitherto, on the freeday, but no Labourer shall thereby be detained later than until 7 þÿo clock a. tn. ; that the attendance on the sick, the keeping of the cattle and the like must he performed by turns, unless some Unfiee of their own accord will undertake to perfoim these duties ;

d, that the Owner, in the crop season shall have preference witli regard to his negroes, it these will work (or hire on the free-day, and he he willing to pay four old bits per day ; but else the Negroes may hire themselves to whomsoever they choose. It is, moreover, Our most gracious will and command, that you cause a school regulation to be drawn up by the juridical Member ol Our þÿWest India Government, in conjunction wnh the Parson and some Planters, as also the provisional organization of schools for the Unfiee in St; Thomas and St. Johns, in analogy to those established in St. Croix, but wiih such modifications, as are rendered necessary by the localities of those Islands, and will you in due tune transmit to Us your report of this matter. The above mentioned Regulations shall he put in practice latest on the 1st of October this year, the necessary measures, with respect to the visiting of the Schools by the Unfrce, having been taken a proper time previously.

For the purpose of relieving the Planters, ii> some degree of the burdens, borne by them, We are most graciously pleased to renounce that part of the Capitation Tax, which is paid into Our T reasury, as We also most graciously approve of, that the extension to the Unfree of all Holy-days, which are considered as such by the Danish Evangelical Congregation in the Colonies, commanded by Our Royal Resolutions of the 1st of May 1840, until further remain suspended. it is Anally Our most gracious pleasure, on account of the rather reduced state of St. þÿJohn L s aiidtreasurv, to bestow from Our Treasury each of the 3 school houses, to be on built on that island, a sum not exceeding 500 Pieces of eight. in intrusting lo you the putting in practice of the dispositions, contained in this Our Royal Rescript, We feel confident, that you will, witn your usual good management, succeed in carrying Our Will into execution, and you will through the medium of Our General Hoard of Customs and Commerce, transmit to Us your report of the result of this matter. Written in Our Royal Residence City oi Copenhagen, 18th of Febuary 1843. Under Our Royal Hand and Seal (Signed) Christian R. To The Governor General of the West India islands.

St. Thomas, 29;h September 1843. The Weather. On Wednesday we experienced in the early part of the day fine weather, a dear skv, with a light breeze from the Southward ami a smooth sea, the Barometer indicated no particular change, until the afternoon when there was a slight variation; the sky became then dark and lowery, the wind freshened but keeping steady to a point of the Compass, the sea was somewhat agitated, and the setting Sun was completely obscured bv heavy clouds; these signs too well announced the approach of a squally or stormy night. At 8 o'clock the weather became tempestuous accompanied with a smart shower, the general aspect at that moment was threatening; and the inhabitants prudently commenced barring and securing their premises, there was a temporary cessation in consequence of the lulling of the wind, but the rain still continued falling þÿ the night was of pitchy darkness save when illumined by the vivid flashes of lightning and distant thunder. We could notice by the distant roaring of the sea, and the loud dashing of the angry surge against the wharves and beach, that there was a heavy Sea in the harbour. The changes in the weather which generally take place during the Equinoctial seasons are generally looked for with dread and alarm bv cverv one, particularly by persons who have witnessed the terrific violence and disastrous effects of the Hurricanes in the West Indies.
